title: The Uncertainty Tax
author: Tonie Marie Gordon
summary: Tonie Marie Gordon argues that the most expensive disruption of the AI transition for organizations is not any particular capability but the condition of not knowing what comes next. She describes a jagged frontier, citing Stanford's 2026 AI Index, in which release schedules, capability jumps and pricing are unpredictable to outside planners, and points to worker sentiment data from Mercer, ADP and the APA showing widespread and largely anticipatory job insecurity. Behavioral science, she argues, has long shown what this condition does to judgment. The analytical core draws on De Berker and colleagues' finding that physiological stress tracks uncertainty and degrades performance, and on Ellsberg-style ambiguity aversion. Organizationally, ambiguity aversion produces two failure modes: pilot purgatory as institutional procrastination and reactive spending as herding. The anxiety response also suppresses the creativity, candor and intelligent risk-taking the moment requires. Her prescription for leaders is to govern uncertainty rather than pretend to resolve it: convert ambiguity into stated risk, name a review cadence, design decisions for reversibility, separate personal security from role uncertainty, and protect experimentation through psychological safety. (Filed as Leadership rather than Technology because the operational target is leaders managing people and decisions under AI uncertainty.)
points: Gordon locates AI's heaviest organizational cost in unpredictability itself, supported by evidence that stress and performance degradation track uncertainty rather than bad outcomes.
Ambiguity aversion explains both endless proof-of-concept pilots (freezing) and copying competitors' AI spending (herding), neither of which is a real strategy under uncertainty.
Chronic job-insecurity anxiety suppresses exploration and candor, creating a self-defeating loop in which disruption degrades the organization's response to disruption.
Leaders can reduce the tax by replacing "we don't know" with bounded statements of what is known, watched, planned for and when it will be revisited.
Structuring AI commitments as reversible options (staged rollouts, low lock-in, swappable models) removes the need for certainty the environment cannot supply.
quotes: The instinct is to treat this as a technology-adoption problem, which makes the issue a matter of keeping pace. That framing misses where the real cost lands. The disruption that matters most is not the arrival of any particular capability. It’s the condition of not knowing what comes next, and behavioral science has been measuring what that condition does to human judgment for a very long time.
The numbers describing worker sentiment aren’t just measuring the impact of AI today, they’re measuring the effect of not knowing its impact tomorrow.

The proof-of-concept theater that analysts described, endless pilots that never convert to production, is ambiguity aversion expressed as institutional procrastination. The reactive spending that outruns governance is the same aversion expressed as herding, the substitution of a peer’s apparent certainty for one’s own absent information.

An anxious workforce narrows, hedges, and conceals. Therefore, the psychological climate produced by the AI transition undermines the adaptive behavior the transition most requires, a self-defeating loop in which the disruption degrades the response to the disruption.

We don’t know” is corrosive. “Here is what we know, here is what we’re watching, here is the range we’re planning against, and here is when we’ll revisit it” converts a formless threat into a specified one the mind can prepare for. The reduction in stress comes from the specification itself, even when the news isn’t good.

Ambiguity aversion is most paralyzing when a choice feels irreversible, because the cost of being wrong is permanent. Structure AI commitments as options rather than bets wherever possible: staged rollouts, contracts that avoid deep lock-in, architectures that assume the underlying model will be swapped.
Certainty about the organization’s posture toward its people is available even when certainty about the technology isn’t.

The psychological safety that underwrites this isn’t a comfort measure. It’s the mechanism by which an organization keeps exploring rather than freezing when the ground is moving, and it’s the direct behavioral counterweight to the inhibition that accompanies uncertainty.
